#3078. Why Texas Pacific Land Stock Was Slumping While the Market Surged Today

The company announced a roughly $3 billion acquisition.

By Eric Volkman – Nov 23, 2026 at 3:01PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Texas Pacific Land ›

On a hot Monday for the stock market, investors were rather cool on Texas Pacific Land (TPL -3.50%) stock. In late-session trading, the land management company's stock was down by nearly 3% after it announced the signing of a $3 billion deal to acquire a peer. The decline of the shares was counter to the general direction of the market; at that point, the benchmark S&P 500 index was up by nearly 5%.

That morning, Texas Pacific announced it has agreed to acquire EagleRock Land (EROK +7.72%) for roughly $3 billion in an all-stock transaction. Like Texas Pacific, EagleRock holds and manages acreage in and around the Permian Basin, a vast area in the Southwest that comprises the largest oil field in the U.S.

Upon closing the deal, the two companies will be merged into a new holding company called Texas Pacific Land Corporation. Shares of the current Texas Pacific will automatically be converted into equity of the new company.

Under the terms of the arrangement, EagleRock shareholders are to receive slightly over 0.08 shares of Texas Pacific Land Corporation for each EagleRock share they own. When the sale is completed, it's estimated that current Texas Pacific investors will own roughly 86% of Texas Pacific Land Corporation, and EagleRock stockholders the remainder.

Texas Pacific's board also authorized a boost to the company's existing common stock buyback program, to a total of $500 million. The company estimates that the annual run rate synergies of owning EagleRock will amount to $45 million. It also believes the merger will be immediately accretive to cash flow per share.

The deal has been unanimously approved by both Texas Pacific's and EagleRock's board of directors. It is subject to approval by the latter company's shareholders. Texas Pacific expects the transaction will close in the first half of 2027.

Texas Pacific's market cap is just under $18 billion, so it's understandable that investors are worried about dilution. But this is quite a complementary asset purchase by the company, and I think its synergies will make the move worthwhile before long.

#3077. IEEE Celebrates 10 Years of Incorporating Ethics Into AI Systems

Standards and certifications foster socially responsible products

Kathy Pretz is the editor in chief of The Institute, IEEE's member publication

Those issues are relatively new to many people, but the IEEE Standards Association has been working for the past decade on ways to prioritize the responsible development of AI systems.

In 2016 IEEE SA launched the IEEE Global Initiative for Ethical Considerations in Autonomous and Intelligent Systems (A/IS) and published the Ethically Aligned Design report. EAD’s mission is to encourage everyone involved in designing autonomous and intelligent systems to prioritize human well-being by applying ethical considerations for the benefit of humanity.

Developed by a multidisciplinary community of experts from around the world, the report outlined eight foundational principles for A/IS. They include human rights, people’s well-being, and transparency. More than 100 leading AI ethics experts provided input. EAD’s Version II report was released in 2017. Both versions solicited public input and received hundreds of pages of feedback, according to John C. Havens, who was the global initiative’s founding executive director, and is now the global director for IEEE Planet Positive 2030. And by 2019, there were more than 400 contributors and the community continues to grow.

“Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE,” Havens says. “At the time it was released, there wasn’t anything like it.”

Since its launch, a series of standards has been developed to provide practical guidelines on designing, building, and deploying technology that prioritizes human values. Several AI ethics certification programs have been introduced.

This year marks the 10th anniversary of EAD’s first draft. To celebrate, IEEE SA recently launched a website, a podcast series, and a blog that reflect on the report’s achievements and impact.

The word ethics is often used interchangeably with morality, but that is not the case in responsible AI systems design, according to EAD’s first version. The report includes insights from classical ethics traditions and value-based design methodologies to offer actionable recommendations for engineers developing AI tools.

The report established eight foundational general principles for designing autonomous and intelligent systems: respecting human rights, prioritizing increased well-being as success criteria for development, empowering individuals with data agency to have control over their identity, effectiveness, transparency, accountability, awareness of misuse, and competence for the system creators.

The principles shift applied ethics to the design stage of AI systems, compared with being a concern after they’re released, the authors wrote.

IEEE SA offers a suite of ethics in AI programs including IEEE CertifAIEd, which includes two certifications: one for individuals and one for products.

The professional certification provides individuals with skills to assess autonomous and intelligent systems for adherence to IEEE’s methodology and ethics criteria.

“Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE.” —John C. Havens, founding executive director of the global initiative

The product certification program assesses whether an organization’s AI tool or system conforms to the criteria in the IEEE Ontological Specifications. A CertifiAIEd assessor evaluates the product to ensure it meets the criteria. Upon completion of the assessment, the owner submits it to the IEEE Conformity Assessment Program, which can certify it and issue the certification mark.

IEEE SA also recently released its Responsible AI for Children certification program. This program certifies that AI products for children have been independently tested and verified to meet design and ethics requirements.

The IEEE Artificial Intelligence Systems (AIS) for Global Flourishing Collaborative Industry Collections group was formed to provide the resources, knowledge, and tools needed to prioritize people’s well-being to developers of AI systems. It has more than 200 members.

The collaborative describes its work as a practical, systems-level framework for responsible technology design that translates flourishing into applied methods, metrics, and tools that can be used throughout the AIS lifecycle.

The group is establishing guidelines for how to design, evaluate, and govern systems that can measurably improve human well-being and ecological sustainability.

Subcommittees are focused on cognition, education, faith, planetary care, spirituality, and other issues.

“The group is building directly off the well-being chapter of Ethically Aligned Design and the IEEE 7010 standard (Recommended Practice for Assessing the Impact of Autonomous and Intelligent Systems on Human Well-Being),” Havens says. “That’s on purpose because if human and planetary flourishing aren’t addressed first in design, then human well-being and planetary sustainability are afterthoughts.”

To mark the 10-year anniversary, IEEE SA created the five-part “Ethically Aligned Design: 10 Years of Impact” podcast series. It launched on 21 October. New episodes are being released every two weeks.

The episodes center around the vision for EAD, the process for selecting its foundational principles, and how they were translated into the IEEE 7000 standards.

The first podcast, “Origins of Ethically Aligned Design,” explored early efforts to make ethics a practical part of AI and autonomous system design. The experts discussed challenges, debates, global collaboration, and the real-world impact that helped move responsible technology from ethical principles toward actionable standards and practices.

The second podcast, “The Chapters and Committees” focuses on the multidisciplinary groups that worked on turning broad human values into practical guidance for AI and autonomous systems.

The podcast discussions serve as material for a thought leadership program that also includes blog articles about the IEEE 7000 series and educational resources to continue to raise awareness and support of this groundbreaking work.

This article was updated on 18 November 2026.

Kathy Pretz is editor in chief for The Institute, which covers all aspects of IEEE, its members, and the technology they're involved in. She has a bachelor's degree in applied communication from Rider University, in Lawrenceville, N.J., and holds a master's degree in corporate and public communication from Monmouth University, in West Long Branch, N.J.

#3076. Google Search’s AI Mode can now read your Wallet, with Drive next

Opt-in connections let Search tap your spending, documents and Gemini chats for personal answers.

Google’s graphic for connecting Wallet, Drive and other apps to Personal Intelligence in Search.

Google is rolling out an opt-in connection between Google Wallet and Personal Intelligence in Search’s AI Mode, with Drive and the Gemini app to follow in the coming weeks. The read-only Wallet link lets AI Mode suggest ways to cut spending and use card rewards.

Google Search’s AI Mode can now use your Google Wallet to give more personal answers, the company announced on Monday. Drive and the Gemini app will follow in the coming weeks. It is the latest step in Google’s AI overhaul of Search, unveiled at I/O in May.

The opt-in connections are part of Personal Intelligence, which already lets AI Mode draw on Gmail, Calendar and Photos. With Wallet linked, AI Mode can suggest ways to trim spending and make the most of cash-back and reward points on cards stored in Wallet. Google says the link is read-only, so AI Mode cannot move, manage or invest money.

With Drive connected, AI Mode can use documents, spreadsheets and PDFs, for example to draw up a plan for tax season. Linking the Gemini app will let ideas explored in one carry over to the other.

Google launched the same Wallet link in Gemini for US users ten days ago, and OpenAI has let some ChatGPT users link bank accounts since May. Users can switch each app on or off under Connected Apps in Search Personalization, and a new icon will show what personal context a response used.

Its compact design and advanced features combine customisable elements with a user-assisted interface that will make it easy to craft delectable espresso.

I've been reviewing coffee makers for over six years, and I never log on for a day of work without two shots of espresso in my system. An SCA-certified barista, I've tested everything from a $9 French press to a $3,000 espresso machine. I'd happily drink a brew made in any of the seven machines I've featured in my carefully-curated list of the best coffee makers. So if you want an expert-approved brewer, just keep scrolling.

It's late November, which means Black Friday deals are live. Our on-page tech in this guide will show you when there are discounts on our favorite machines, but if you're looking for more coffee deals over the holiday season, we're continually updating our roundup of the best Black Friday deals, including coffee makers like the Keurig K-Express which is almost half price right now. Or, if you're after inspiration for the enthusiast in your life, these are the best gifts for coffee lovers this holiday season.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

We've reviewed nearly a dozen coffee makers so far this year, and most notably, reviewer Erin re-tested the iconic Moccamaster, which we last put through its paces back in 2021. We wanted to see if it still held its own against the many outstanding releases of the last few years. And the answer is a resounding yes. Now back at the top of our guide, it's certainly the one to beat for the rest of the year's top releases.

Compiling this buying guide has required a lot of evaluation and comparison between completely unrelated methods of brewing, as well as machines that span from $50 to well over $2,000. How, you might wonder, can we rank these machines if they're being tested against completely different criteria?

It's true, I'd never tell you to buy a drip coffee maker if you love espresso, and we'd never tell you to buy the most premium machine if you're on a budget, so before you buy, you need to have a rough idea of what kind of coffee you actually want to make at home.

In this guide, I've included drip coffee makers, as well as a range of single-serve machines and espresso machines. And when ranking these products, I've considered what's right for most people. I know a lot more about coffee than the majority of buyers, so I had to go back to basics when writing this guide to make it accessible to everyone.

Even within the Tom's Guide team, there's a huge range of coffee preferences. There are some people who would turn their nose up at a cup of pod coffee, and would never consider straying from their carefully evaluated coffee setup.

For others, coffee is simply a tool for waking up in the morning, and you just want a reliable and space-efficient gadget to fill your cup with something cheaper and better than the stuff you'd get from a chain coffee shop. That's ok too, because you know your budget, and you know what you're looking for. And no matter what it is that you're seeking, I'm confident that I've included it in this guide.

Each and every machine has been hand-selected and tested by myself or one of Tom's Guide's expert testers, so you can click through to read full, detailed reviews before you make up your mind.

The Technivorm Moccamaster KBGV Select has been in this buying guide for five years, but a lot has changed since our first review in 2021. So in early 2026, we took it for another spin to see if it can hold its own against the latest and greatest releases.

Well, the results are in, and the Moccamaster is still the cream of the crop. Hand-made in the Netherlands, the brand has a well-deserved reputation for quality construction and dependable results. It's not the cheapest option, but if you treat it with care, it will last a lifetime.

Reviewer Erin said "the Moccamaster is so famous because nothing really compares. Nothing comes close. The Moccamaster has been topping “best-of” lists before best-of lists were even a thing — it’s reigned supreme since the ‘60s."

Compared to feature-rich options like the Ratio Four, Breville Luxe Brewer, or OXO Brew 8-Cup, the Moccamaster stands out for its simplicity and efficiency. It forgoes extras like cold brew modes or app controls, but it’s faster than the Ratio Four, easier to use than the Breville Luxe Brewer, and delivers a more consistent cup than the OXO. The machine offers simplicity and ease of use in everyday drip brewing.

To use, simply add your water to the tank and your grounds to the filter, and switch it on. However, it's this simplicity that has earned special recognition from the Specialty Coffee Association. Using a copper heating element and precise brew temperature control, the KBGV Select can hit industry-standard temperatures between 196°F and 205°F in under a minute and, crucially, stay there throughout the entire brewing process. The gentle showerhead-style water dispenser will evenly agitate coffee grounds to create a balanced extraction.

The Breville Bambino Plus has been on the market for seven years, but it's still one of the most popular espresso machines ever released. If you're based in Europe (like me) you'll know this brand as Sage, but the machines are otherwise the same.

With groundbreaking automatic steaming technology, which is still top of the line nearly a decade later, this is the espresso machine for you if you're in the market for an entry-level machine with some serious power.

We made some outstanding shots of espresso with this gadget. I'm talking drool-worthy toffee-colored strands of crema and a vibrant extraction that tasted fantastic. You should note, this machine doesn't have a grinder built in.

You'll want to pair it with one of the best coffee grinders (you can buy a good one for around $100, and our reviews walk you through all the options) for the ideal espresso, but if you use a double-walled portafilter you can still achieve a lively brew when using pre-ground coffee.

As for the automatic milk steaming, this thing can achieve a very fine micro-foam that's totally latte art-worthy, completely hands-free. And it automatically purges after each use, which will keep the steam wand clog-free and running smoothly (so long as you descale regularly).

If you want a single-serve coffee maker that can truly do it all, you should look no further than the Nespresso Vertuo Lattissima. Featuring a separate milk dispenser that offers milk-only drinks and two lengths of milk add-ins to any coffee size you opt for, the beauty of this machine is in its simplicity.

You can simply store the milk dispenser in the refrigerator when it's not in use, and you'll get the joys of the entirety of Nespresso's six-size Vertuo system if you prefer a long black coffee or an espresso to start the day.

We enjoyed the thoughtful touches such as an adjustable cup holder to work with any beverage size, and the ability to rinse out the milk dispenser after each use. We did wish that there were more than one milk froth level available, because if you prefer a firmer layer to make an espresso or a softer latte-style steamed milk, you won't be able to adjust this using the Nespresso.

Because this machine is part of the Vertuo line it will automatically brew the optimum drink length for each drink and you can enjoy an ever-evolving list of capsules to mix up your routine. We even tried a cold-brew capsule, which was impressively realistic.

Sometimes, simple is better. The OXO Brew 8-Cup is one such machine. It's shy on buttons and limited on features, but this machine undeniably makes tasty coffee, and it's SCA-certified to prove it.

You can brew either 2-4 cups or 5-8 cups with the OXO Brew. It simply requires you to fill up the water tank to your desired cup amount, load up a filter and coffee grounds, then hit start.

There's beauty in the simplicity, though. Its rainshower distribution ensures that grounds are soaked evenly and consistently before extraction, meaning you won't be left with anemic or muddy coffee, and your coffee will never taste burnt from uncontrolled water temperatures.

Another plus is the double-walled carafe. This will keep your brew hot for a couple of hours, making it ideal for busy households. Reviewer Camryn's only complaint was the water tank, which can't be removed. That's annoying, but it's nothing a jug can't fix.

Somehow, the De'Longhi La Specialista Touch manages to be both super-smart and aesthetically pleasing, while also compact enough for small kitchens. It's no mean feat, and one that won the machine the top spot in our best espresso machine buying guide.

The main addition is the responsive 3.5-inch touchscreen, which walks you through everything from dialing in your beans (finding the right grind size for your specific brew) to automatically steaming the milk for the drink of your choosing.

While there are plenty of excellent automatic features here, this machine also lets you take the reins, which will be a welcome feature for those who want to work on their home barista skills. I enjoyed hand-steaming with this machine, and was able to toggle with finer features to really master every espresso.

It's a small feature, but De'Longhi should take a bow for how compact the La Specialista Touch is. It slotted easily onto my countertops, which often look drowned by larger coffee makers. And despite its compact size, it still does literally everything you could want from an espresso machine.

While it looks like a drip coffee maker, the Ratio Four is actually an automated pour-over coffee maker. So if you love pour-over, but don't love the laborious process of brewing it, the Ratio Four is for you.

With a sleek, minimalist appearance and straightforward operation, the Ratio took just under seven minutes to brew a 20-ounce serving of coffee, and one cup was complete in three and a half minutes.

Reviewer Erin recommends this option for serious coffee lovers. She called it "sophisticated enough to excite even the most fastidious coffee shop hipster," noting that "if you’re familiar with coffee bean varieties and the phrases “pre-infusion” and “optimal flow rate” don’t scare you off, this is the machine for you."

The main downside of this brewer is its lack of 'keep warm' setting. Unlike your average drip brewer, it's not designed with bulk brewing in mind. This one's for the true coffee enthusiasts, who would never dream of reheating a precious V60 brew. If you do want a keep-warm option, check out the Moccamaster or Breville Luxe.

The Terra Kaffe Demi is a standout choice for those who want café-quality drinks at home with zero fuss. Its intuitive interface and one-touch operation make espresso simple, so you can enjoy impressive coffee without mastering barista skills or fiddling with settings.

There are downsides to superautomatic espresso machines, which is why few have scored highly in our rigorous Barista-led testing. But where the locked-away grinding, brewing and steaming mechanisms may feel restrictive for coffee enthusiasts, if your key concern is reliability and ease of use, you can't go wrong with the likes of the Terra Kaffe.

Machines that require manual tamping or careful monitoring, such as the De'Longhi La Specialista Touch, can't match the Demi's ease of use. Simply press a button, add your beans, and it will craft anything from a piping hot espresso to a long black Americano in minutes. There's one major con: it doesn't have a milk frother, which many superautomatic machines from the likes of Jura and De'Longhi do offer.

For anyone who wants the easiest possible coffee routine, the Demi’s accessible cleaning features are a relief. After a month of daily use, review Dan found maintenance practically painless. Pop out the brew group for a rinse, and you’re done. If you want hands-off, great-tasting espresso with minimal upkeep, the Demi delivers. But if you're a coffee lover who knows their arabica from their robusta, its lack of customisation may prove frustrating.

I joined Tom's Guide in 2024 on the product reviews team. While I test everything from keyboards to vacuum cleaners, I'm also a former barista with years and years of experience, which is why I'm Tom's Guide's go-to coffee maker tester.

I've tested a number of leading espresso machines from Smeg and KitchenAid, as well as other brewing methods such as the AeroPress. I've also been down to Smeg and La Pavoni HQ to get hands-on with some high-tech gear.

I’m Tom’s Guide's Reviews Editor and I’ve been an espresso enthusiast for almost a decade now.

As a former chef, I started using commercial espresso machines to make tiramisu while working in an Italian restaurant, and that’s where my fascination with 9-bar pressure began. And it hasn’t stopped since.

These days, I spend large chunks of my day testing out the latest and greatest coffee gear, from coffee grinders and weighing scales through to pour-over drippers and, of course, coffee machines.

At the end of the day, the most important sign of a good coffee maker comes down to that all-important taste test. So it goes without saying that I taste a lot of coffee when putting together my coffee maker reviews. However, there are endless factors that can determine the flavor of your finished coffee, so there are some metrics I need to consider (and keep consistent) when testing coffee makers and curating buying guides.

The most sustainable choice you can make when buying a new coffee maker is opting for a machine that will last for years and years. That said, it's a good sign when a coffee maker comes in recyclable, sustainable packaging that still keeps it secure during shipping, so I'm always looking out for this when evaluating my first impressions of a product.

In my experience, a more drawn-out setup process can be worth the extra hassle. Some coffee makers have a water hardness strip included to input the limescale level in your water. This test takes a few extra minutes, but inputting this information will ensure the machine reminds you to descale it as and when needed to prolong its lifespan.

If a coffee maker comes with an app or any bespoke programming such as personalized profiles or pre-set timers, we troubleshoot this in testing to make sure you're getting an easy-to-use machine from the very first use.

Coffee makers don't have to be expensive — especially if you're buying a single-serve or drip coffee maker, but it's often the case that you get what you pay for with coffee makers. When testing I evaluate if this is the case. Does a $1,000+ coffee maker really warrant the price tag, and most importantly, would I recommend it to a friend or family member who was shopping for a new machine?

Your cup of coffee can only be as good as the grounds you use, so when testing, I try and opt for an accessible consumer blend and stick to this brand across models to ensure that the differences we taste in our coffee come from the quality of the machine, and not the beans.

As a basic rule, I use fresh-roasted arabica beans in every review. This allows the taste and extraction of every coffee to shine through. And while I don't expect that every home tester will be splashing out on artisan beans, at least this way you know you're getting a machine that can create some seriously tasty coffee if you ever decide to level up from those kilo bags of robusta.

This is particularly important for drip coffee makers. I test the temperature of each carafe I make when it's first brewed, and then after one hour, to test the quality of the heating plate on each machine.

If freshly brewed coffee comes out too hot, it's a sign that the machine has scorched the grounds in testing, which will result in a more bitter flavor and is a sign of a poorly-made machine. Likewise, if the coffee is not hot enough, you won't get a fully developed flavor and your coffee will be weak and acidic.

Some coffee makers come with in-built grinders, so I put them through a similar process to our standalone reviews for the best coffee grinders. This involves testing the variety of grind sizes available, and how suitable this is for the type of coffee maker you're using. If your espresso maker's grinder creates great grounds for filter coffee, that's not much help!

I use a coffee sifter called Kruve to see how consistent the coffee grounds are in size and texture, and we also test coffee grinders for static.

If an espresso machine comes with a hand milk steamer, there is an inevitable margin for user error when testing. Fortunately, I have a team of expert testers on-hand who have steamed more than a few lattes in their time, so if they find fault with a steamer, I can confidently say it's a flaw in design.

When steaming milk, I look for a smooth and fine micro-foam that doesn't burn the milk before we're able to get the consistency we want.

Some machines come with automatic frothers, and while it's hard for these to recreate a hand-steaming effect, I look for how easy they are to use and how close they come to the real thing.

If all of this seems a bit overwhelming, we've tried to simplify the category a bit and help you decide on which type of coffee maker you should buy.

We test a lot of coffee makers. It feels like there's always a new innovation to put through its paces, so our testing team can be found reliably caffeinated on any given day.

We return most of the coffee makers we test due to the high value of these machines, but on the occasion that we're allowed to keep one, we continue to test them from home in order to evaluate the value for money over time, and compare our old faithfuls to recent releases.

Not every coffee maker can make the list though. Here are some of the models we've recently tried.

The xBloom is one of the most interesting drip coffee makers on the market, with legions of fans who love getting involved with every step of the brewing process.

Read the full xBloom Drip Coffee Maker review

Let's just say Erin did not enjoy the Gevi. Its in-built grinder is really, really bad, which means it's impossible to get a decent brew out of this machine.

Read the full Gevi 10-Cup Drip Coffee Maker review

Smeg EMC02 Mini Pro Manual Espresso Machine (★★★★☆)

Smeg teamed up with La Pavoni, makers of the original espresso machine, to create the EMC02. And it lives up to the hype. In testing, Erin found that it's the closest she's got to professional equipment at home.

Read the full Smeg EMC02 Mini Pro Manual Espresso Machine review

Erin described the De'Longhi Rivelia as a coffee-making robot. This superautomatic does it all, from grinding your beans to order to frothing just the right amount of milk for your desired drink. Its smart interface is what sets it apart, with different user profiles allowing you to interact with the machine depending on everything from your go-to drink to the time of day. We couldn't add it to the guide because, while it's very well-priced in the U.K., the price in America is a bit exorbitant for what you get.

Cheap and plasticky the Stilosa may be, but we found that it's capable of making a mean cup of coffee. The espresso took some manual adjustments, but the flavor rivalled shots we've pulled in much more expensive machines. We don't recommend it for beginners, but if you're on a budget and are willing to put in the hours, it's a good option.

There's only so good Nespresso coffee can taste, so you may as well get one of the brand's cheaper machines, especially if you're not concerned with milk-based drinks. The Pop+ is compact and cute to look at, but it drips a lot and won't fit every mug. If you're looking for a neat little machine, it's a savvy option — especially if you find it on sale.

Amazon-favorite brand Casabrews offers suspiciously affordable espresso machines which certainly look the part, but can they deliver? Surprisingly, they kind of can. Don't get me wrong, they won't compete with the Breville Bambino Plus, but for the price, it's a great entry-level option. Admittedly, its steam wand is a bit subpar.

The Oracle Dual Boiler is Breville's latest, and dare we say, greatest release. It's massively expensive: $3,000, which makes it a tough machine to recommend. This superpowered brewer offers pro-level specs, but reviewer Pete didn't love the grinder.

You won't find a Keurig in this guide. Compared to the myriad options on the market, I just couldn't bring myself to recommend this restrictive and bitterly dark-roasted coffee brand to the average shopper. But some people love Keurig, and we've got a dedicated best Keurig coffee maker guide just for those people. The K-Duo Hot & Iced is the winner in that guide, scoring a 4.5-star review.

Philips Barista Brew Espresso Machine (★★★☆☆)

The Philips Barista Brew is the brand's latest innovation: a semi-automatic machine that features a separate grinder and brewing unit. In testing we were very impressed with the espresso we made in this machine, but the milk steaming was lacking.

Read the full Philips Barista Brew Espresso Machine review

This super-smart coffee makers is one of the niftiest and quietest machines we've tested, but the eye-watering price tag means we'd struggle to recommend it to most people. It's certainly one of the most premium appliances we've tested in some time, and ideal for those on a large budget who enjoy a high-tech setup.

Cuisinart Grind and Brew Single Serve (★★★★☆)

This Cuisinart single-serve coffee maker comes with a K-cup sized filter and a grinder that can refill your reusable filter with freshly ground beans for each use. It's a great, sustainable idea, but in practice a bit fiddly. If you're committed to single-serve but want to keep things sustainable, it's a good option.

The Rancilio Silvia is beautiful and well-suited to coffee enthusiasts who want to mod their own machine, but user-friendly it is not. Our reviewer Pete is a real pro, but even he said you'd need to put in a lot of work to get this machine brewing beautiful espressos. It's not bad, but it's not right for the average shopper.

The Philips 3200 Series LatteGo used to be in this guide, but it was ousted by the KitchenAid KF8 for its superior quality espresso and easy controls. We're currently reviewing Philips' latest LatteGo machine though, so this line could make a comeback.

Read the full Philips 3200 Series LatteGo review

If you have the cash to splash, you will get a semi-automatic espresso machine that's both easy to use and deeply customizable with the Fellow Espresso. Its ability to steam non-dairy milks is especially impressive, with the only minor issue being its damp coffee pucks being hard to clean up.

Read the full Fellow Espresso Series 1 review

Simply Good Coffee Plastic-Free Brewer (★★★★☆)

The no-frills design and simple but effective drip brewing of SGC's coffee maker is held back by its price. Also, the "plastic-free" claim only applies to the interior components, which is a little misleading if you're keen to minimize plastics in your life.

Read the full Simply Good Coffee Plastic-Free Brewer review

Ninja's coffee maker wants to be your one-stop shop for all kinds of coffee drinks. But not all its creations are of equal quality, with cold drinks suffering in particular.

Read the full Ninja AutoBarista Pro review

This little coffee maker is a great option if you're looking for something to fit into a student dorm or a smaller kitchen. Unfortunately, the coffee that it produces tastes a little flat and isn't as tasty as similarly price competition.

There’s nothing like a great cup of coffee to wake you up in the morning, so if you’re looking to invest in a new coffee maker, you’ll want one that makes the ideal brew, provides the functionality and practicality you desire and comes in on budget. Here are a few things you’ll need to think about.

Will it fit?A coffee maker sits on the countertop, so measure the space where you plan to keep the machine before you buy one. Be sure to determine the clearance between the countertop and the bottom of your cabinets. Most, but not all coffee makers will fit under a cabinet.

Coffee qualityIf you're passionate about coffee, look for a brewer that says it meets the Specialty Coffee Association's Golden Cup Standard. This means the coffee brews at what is regarded as the perfect time and temperature for the best cup of Joe.

But be aware that this standard calls for using 2 tablespoons of ground coffee for each 5-ounce cup, which produces a very full-bodied, strong cup of coffee that is not to everyone's taste.

Brewing coffee at home does mean you'll have a lot of spent grounds around, but instead of putting them in the trash, there are plenty of ways you can reuse old coffee grounds.

Cup sizeKeep in mind that coffee-maker cups are the equivalent of 5 ounces, or an old-fashioned teacup that isn't filled to the brim, leaving room for milk. Most coffee mugs in use today hold upward of 8 ounces. Therefore, a typical 12-cup coffee maker brews enough coffee for about seven mugs at the most.

What kind of carafe?Models with thermal carafes tend to be more expensive than those with glass carafes. You can bring thermal carafes to the table, where they'll keep coffee hot for refills. However, these carafes have narrow openings that are difficult to hand-wash, and most can't be cleaned in the dishwasher. However, thermal carafes are beneficial if you drink coffee throughout the day.

Milk frotherIf you prefer your coffee straight, you won’t be concerned about the milk frother option, although do consider that other household members or guests may prefer their coffee served with a smooth froth. Having a milk frother combined will also save you the issue of having a separate appliance on the countertop, taking up space.

Paper or permanent filters? Decide if you want to use a permanent filter or paper, disposable ones. Permanent filters are better for the environment, and you don't have to constantly replace them, but they do need to be thoroughly washed by hand and they tend to stain.

Also, it's easier to toss paper filters in the trash than knock grounds out of a metal filter. You may also find that the taste of the coffee produced differs depending on filter type and that you prefer one over the other.

Do you want to set it and forget it? With many machines, you can program them ahead of time to brew in the morning or right before you get home, and you can even set them to brew at the same time every day. But such features add to the price and work only if you take the time to read the manual and figure out how to use the setting.

If you're looking for a drip coffee maker, one of the best indicators of quality is an SCA Gold Cup Standard certification. The SCA (Specialty Coffee Association) awards this to machines that brew a 1:16 to 1:18 ratio (that's parts coffee to water) and within a specific temperature range of 196 and 205 degrees Fahrenheit.

Typically, machines that meet this specification are ideally designed to deliver a good cup of coffee. Every drip machine within this guide is SCA-certified, too.

Looking for an espresso machine? Don't pay much attention to the number of bars of pressure it offers. Anything over nine will suffice, as this is the amount of pressure required to make espresso. Instead, consider the number of grind settings on any included grinders, as a quality grinder should allow for plenty of customization. For most people, an in-built PID controller will assist you in getting that perfect extraction.

If you're looking for a bean-to-cup coffee machine, you're likely in the market for a superautomatic, meaning you can press a button and it will grind and brew your drink using fully automatic internal systems.

We've tested a number of bean-to-cup machines, and our top pick is the Terra Kafe Demi, which works fast and creates balanced, evenly-extracted brews. Its in-built milk frothing is also up to scratch if you enjoy a frothy coffee, although it'll never rival a hand-steamed latte.

If you want to create a range of milk-based espresso drinks, you should opt for something with a separate steam wand. I'd suggest you check out the Ninja Luxe Café Pro, which has a separate steam wand with both manual and automatic steaming.

If you opt for automatic, the wand will texturize your milk to your desired level and according to the type of milk (dairy, oat, almond, etc) you choose. There's even a menu on the side of the machine which guides you through the different milk settings, and which to use depending on your desired drink.

My hot take is that you'll have a longer-lasting coffee setup if you opt for a separate brewer and one of the best coffee grinders, but if you want an in-built grinder, there are some good options out there.

If you want an espresso machine, a quality grinder is especially important, as your beans will need to be ground very finely to achieve a quality extraction. As a general rule, I trust Breville machines to grind well, and I also had a great experience with the "Bean Adapt" tech in the De'Longhi La Specialista Touch.

#3073. Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO of Nvidia, stock up 30%

Nvidia has announced that disgraced CEO Jensen Huang has been reinstated to the role, effective immediately. The company’s share price jumped more than 30% in response, with the rest of the market also making significant gains.

It said that the board voted unanimously in favor of reinstatement despite its recent statement that it had no intention of doing so …

Huang’s affair with a woman suspected to be a Chinese spy became the main headline news in the tech press after coming to light at the end of last month. The New York Times broke the story on October 29, citing it then as “a close relationship.” Nvidia initially denied that the relationship was anything out of the ordinary.

That changed on November 8 when Huang publicly admitted to the affair. Nvidia’s shares dropped 5%, and the company’s board of directors opened an independent investigation. Further details emerged over the following days. Things got even worse when the same paper reported that Huang had also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him.

That led to Huang being fired resigning on November 12.

Despite putting the company at enormous risk and initially lying to its board of directors, there were calls in some quarters for Huang to be reinstated. He responded by saying that he would be “honored” to return if asked to do so.

The board of directors, however, said that it had no intention of inviting him back.

Nvidia’s chair Harvey Jones said: “The board does not intend to reinstate him.”

That changed today, with the company making the announcement in a press release.

Nvidia today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”

As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.

The company’s stock price jumped by more than 30% in response, with the rest of the market also up per Yahoo Finance.

#3072. Over 150 child safety groups urge Amazon and eBay to drop AI toys

A Fairplay-led coalition wants AI chatbot toys off sale until independent testing proves them safe, with an answer before Christmas.

A global coalition of more than 150 child safety groups and experts has asked Amazon and eBay to stop selling toys with built-in AI chatbots. The request came in an open letter sent on Monday to Amazon CEO Andy Jassy and eBay CEO Jamie Iannone.

The campaign is led by the nonprofit Fairplay, joined by groups such as Zero to Three and Jonathan Haidt’s Anxious Generation Movement, with signatories from every continent except Antarctica. The letter notes that over 50 AI toys were recently found on sale on Amazon in the US.

The groups want the toys pulled “this holiday season and until they are proven safe.”

The letter argues the two marketplaces already remove unsafe products, so suspending the listings is well within their power. Beyond that, it asks the companies to warn customers of the dangers. Moreover, the campaigners want a public answer before Christmas, so they can take their case to governments and parents.

Amazon has already moved a little, and the company said it removed some AI toys that NBC News and a consumer group had recently tested.

Pressure is coming from several directions at once, as a group of parliamentarians wrote to the two companies earlier this month with the same demand. Some retailers and toy makers have also started pulling AI toys of their own accord.

The campaign also marks an escalation, as last year, Fairplay and its allies simply told parents not to buy the toys; this year, they are going after the shelves themselves.

#3071. Jensen Huang Is Back at Nvidia. These Are 3 Remaining Concerns With Nvidia and What They Mean for the Stock.

Investors are breathing a sigh of relief, but Nvidia is not completely out of the woods.

By Will Healy – Nov 23, 2026 at 3:10PM EST

The return of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia (NVDA +31.48%) is welcome news to shareholders. The stock was up more than 30% in early Monday trading as Huang's reinstatement removed a major source of uncertainty.

However, Huang's return creates new uncertainties or brings existing ones to light. Here are three concerns investors need to watch and whether Nvidia can prosper now that Huang is back.

Jensen Huang. Image source: Getty Images.

Despite Huang's return, the board's probe goes on. The board appointed a committee comprised of independent directors to investigate the CEO's behavior and retained independent counsel to assist. This inquiry proceeds with Huang's approval.

Moreover, the federal government continues to review the matter. Although President Trump remained supportive of Huang, the FBI continues to investigate Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), whom a U.S. official linked to Chinese state security.

Additionally, the U.S. Congress is also conducting its own investigation. To that end, Jensen Huang will testify before congressional committees on Dec. 1.

Hence, while Nvidia's shareholders reacted well to the reinstatement, investors should remember he could still face repercussions for his behavior.

Furthermore, the current members of the board of directors likely face an uncertain future. As mentioned, the board continues to investigate Huang.

Unfortunately, the rush to judgment on Jensen Huang's fate could easily bring repercussions for the board itself.

Admittedly, boards tend to fire employees for having an inappropriate relationship with subordinates. Also, since its job is to focus on a company's affairs, the alleged affair with Nvidia's VP of healthcare, Kimberly Powell, is probably more concerning to them than the indiscretion with the alleged Chinese spy.

Nonetheless, the board is not legally required to terminate executives for such relationships. Moreover, it pressured Huang to resign even though the investigations had not been completed. Since the board lacked a succession plan, it made a move that created tremendous uncertainty for shareholders.

For now, no word has come down on the fate of various board members, but investors should probably be as watchful of their fate as they are of Jensen Huang's.

Jensen Huang's return also puts a spotlight on one of the concerns about his leadership: circular financing.

Huang and CFO Colette Kress have avoided using this term. However, as securing funding has become more difficult, the company has financially backstopped many of its customers. This included a $250 billion backstop for OpenAI that Kress negotiated down to $105 billion.

Concerns about OpenAI's financing have weighed on the stocks of partners such as Oracle (ORCL +12.34%). Also, longtime investors may also recall that circular financing devastated companies during the dot-com boom. At that time, Cisco (CSCO +6.80%) took a $2.25 billion write-down in 2001. Customer bankruptcies hit the company so hard that it traded below its all-time high for more than 25 years.

Nvidia's financial strength may help it avert a decades-long downturn. Nonetheless, similar customer bankruptcies could end the bull market in Nvidia stock.

Despite these concerns, Jensen Huang's return as CEO is, and will likely remain, bullish for Nvidia's shareholders.

Amid these worries, there is no obvious replacement for Huang, and the company (and probably the AI industry as a whole) would likely face years of uncertainty without his vision.

Moreover, Huang's position in the company is likely to be solidified by recent events. Amid the ongoing investigations, investors had to face the possibility of an Nvidia without Huang, and despite the circular financing concerns, they did not like what that looked like.

Ultimately, Huang is unlikely to be forced out again unless the findings of those inquiries leave the company with no choice but to remove him. Consequently, shareholders who held the semiconductor stock throughout the turmoil have been and probably will continue to be rewarded.

#3070. Build a Personal Brand to Help Employers Find You

Routine posting leaves a trail of breadcrumbs for recruiters to discover

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!In one year, the number of developers working for themselves has more than doubled. Stack Overflow’s annual survey of more than 30,000 developers showed that freelancers and sole proprietors went from about four percent of respondents to ten percent.

You can read this as a polite way of saying, “I got laid off and I’m figuring it out.” But I don’t think the number can be ignored.

Whatever the case, it leads to the question I keep hearing from engineers right now: What can I do to stay employable? One tried and true answer is to build a personal brand.

Over the last six years, I grew my LinkedIn audience to 40,000 followers and YouTube channel to 10,000. I don’t think you should aim to be famous (unless you’re into that sort of thing) but I do think it’s worth exploring how to be discoverable online in 2027 if you want an advantage in the open market.

Strip away the follower counts and the AI-generated thought leadership, and a personal brand comes down to a simple question: Does the internet know who you are? When a hiring manager goes looking for someone who has your skills, do you show up?

You can think of this as search engine optimization for your employability. Recruiters have mostly consolidated around a single platform to find people: LinkedIn.

Those 40,000 followers and millions of impressions came with barely a viral post to my name. Nobody is begging me to do sponsorships. But I rarely have trouble finding work, and far more opportunities come to me than I go looking for. That has much less to do with fame than with being easy to find.

You don’t need 10,000 followers. You need a trail of breadcrumbs.

LinkedIn is notorious for being overrun with AI-generated posts. It’s become a running joke. That’s good news for you, because the bar to stand out is “sound like a human being.”

Write about what you actually achieved: a hairy bug you squashed, how your team handles deployments, why you picked some obscure library, the migration that went sideways at 2 a.m. Specifics are hard to fake and easy to trust. (But be careful not to post sensitive information.)

And post a picture of yourself once in a while. People connect with faces a lot faster than with walls of text.

Posts with an opinion tend to outperform tutorials, but you don’t have to dunk on anyone to have one. For instance, if you work on a tech stack people love to mock (VB, .NET, some ancient Java monolith held together with prayer), try something like “What people get wrong about .NET.”

You’ll attract a few trolls in the comments—free engagement, honestly—plus people who want an actual conversation. These comments can turn into actual connections and even… friends.

Posting twice a week is not a big ask. Pick a simple, repeatable format so you’re never staring at an empty text box: what you worked on, what broke, and what you learned. Even a post that gets 10 views leaves one more breadcrumb about who you are and what you know.

Over time, the people who comment become your network. And because so few engineers post about their work on LinkedIn, you can become a big fish in a small pond surprisingly fast.

The best audience is engineers one or two steps behind where you are now. Answer the questions you had a year ago. It helps them, it sharpens your own thinking, and every so often it turns into mentorship in both directions.

It also tells a future employer more about how you think than any résumé bullet ever could.

The engineers who grab the most opportunities are the ones employers can find. You don’t need to become an influencer to be one of them. You just need to leave enough breadcrumbs that the right person can follow them back to you.

AI has made it easier to access information in different domains, but specialist knowledge and human judgement still serve an essential role. Today, an engineer’s core value comes from knowing how to ask the right questions—not from knowing everything.
