What happens when a coffee enthusiast and a professional barista review and rank espresso machines? This guide, that's what.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I bought the wrong espresso machine once, and it was an expensive mistake. With a taste for great coffee but limited knowledge of how to make it, I found one that looked good, had great reviews, and was on sale, and took the plunge. While it was a beautiful machine, it required far too much know-how for a newbie like me to get the most out of it.

Now that I'm a Specialty Coffee Association-qualified barista, it's easy to see where I went wrong. There are so many coffee makers on the market, and for the average first-time buyer, there's a lot of dense terminology to wade through.

That's why I've put this guide together: it breaks down my tried-and-tested recommendations for the best espresso machines you can buy, but also walks you through the things you need to know before you buy a machine, as well as how to get the most out of each option.

There are three main types of domestic espresso machines — manual, automatic, and superautomatic — and each is suited to a different type of buyer. For confident home baristas who want a good machine and don't want to spend too much, the Breville Bambino will be your best friend. But if you want that extra bit of assistance, I think the De'Longhi La Specialista Touch is the best espresso machine for most people.

Black Friday events are in full swing, which means there are plenty of deals on our favorite machines. We're keeping tabs on all the latest discounts in our best Black Friday deals roundup (and on plenty of other great tech we've tested). Or if you're holiday shopping, these are the best gifts for coffee lovers we recommend right now.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

If I was starting from scratch in my small kitchen, this is the machine I'd buy. The De'Longhi La Specialista Touch is strikingly compact and well-priced, but it doesn't skip out on smart features. Striking an ideal balance between user-friendly design and elevated touches, the La Specialista Touch walks you through every part of the brewing process with its responsive 3.5-inch touchscreen.

You can steam milk manually or use automatic features which this machine, which is a welcome feature that brings it into line with much more expensive options from the likes of Breville. In terms of cost, while it's an investment, I think the La Specialista Touch offers outstanding value.

It's fun to make espresso from scratch, but grinding, tamping and brewing can be a messy business. The La Specialista Touch doesn't have an in-built tamping arm, but it does include a tamping kit which allows you to check the volume of your grind and evenly compress it into a puck. The screw-on funnel helps keep things mess-free.

The La Specialista Touch is super interactive, starting at the bean grinding settings. It uses De'Longhi's "Bean Adapt" tech, which walks you through the grinding process by asking you about the type of beans you're grinding and the color, which can indicate the roast level. Based on that, it asks you to set your grinder to a specific number, and then asks you to use the smart tamper to tell the machine the amount of coffee it needs to grind to get the perfect level.

Following all of that, the machine then tells you to increase of decrease grind size depending on how long the extraction takes. Combine all those factors, and it tackles the cause of most bad espressos right from the start.

You can choose from 15 coarseness settings, which is pretty average for machines of this spec and price. It was capable of finely grinding light-roast beans, and there's plenty of scope to increase the grind size for darker roasts.

I made some yummy espresso with the La Specialista Touch. It allows you to save bean settings to shortcut the Bean Adapt process, and I was able to flip between my go-to Lost Sheep Get To The Hopper beans and some cheap Aldi beans with ease.

When using great beans, the machine delivered a rich brew with notes of toffee and chocolate. It was the ultimate base for a latte or cappuccino, and if I was making an americano, I could leave my cup in place for the machine to top it up with hot water using a dispenser located right next to the group head.

I should also note that this machine makes cold brew, which is an increasingly popular feature in more modern machines. My brew was light, fruity, and balanced, but you should note that it doesn't brew cold espresso.

You can steam milk both manually and automatically with this machine, but I have a preference for manual steaming. Its included (useful) temperature gauge prevents your milk from burning, but it also gets in the way a little when hand-steaming. I got used to it, but it was a minor annoyance at first.

As for the automatic milk steaming, this was among some of the best I've tried. If I'm being picky, this is a feature I think Breville machines dominae, but the La Specialista Touch did make some fantastic latte milk which poured well with some swirling. My cappuccino foam was light and a little dry, which made a great topper to a shot of rich espresso.

We don't give out five-star reviews often, but Breville's cheapest coffee maker is hard to fault. Featuring the stainless steel exterior and quality construction we expect from Breville, it features a cost-conscious price tag that those familiar with the brand may not expect.

Espresso machines can be chunky, so this is a rare compact option that will sit streamlined in just about any space. It's one of the few options in this guide that doesn't include a grinder, so you'll have to use pre-ground coffee or purchase your own grinder (check out our reviews of the best coffee grinders for some options, but they don't have to be expensive!) to use it.

Reviewer Erin said "Damn, this is such a good machine. This machine’s functionality vs. cost is darn near unbelievable" when she tested it, and called the espresso she made in the Bambino "delectable".

This machine doesn't have a grinder, but it's worth digging into why that's not a bad thing. For a start, some enthusiasts prefer to buy separate grinders and espresso machines as it allows them to switch up their setup more easily, and if something breaks, you won't have to replace your entire coffee setup.

The machine comes with single-walled and double-walled baskets. If you plan on using pre-ground coffee, I'd suggest starting with double-walled, as they can bring back some of the fresh and lively flavor you'll be missing from fresh-ground coffee.

The Breville Bambino produces very high-quality espresso without taking up too much counter space. Breville (or Sage, for European readers) is famed for making market-leading machines, and while this is one of the brand's entry-level options, it doesn't miss out on premium-feeling features or the powerful extraction you'll need to get a great shot.

There's pre-infusion, which will soak your puck to allow flavors to develop before extracting your shot, and there's also volumetric dispensing to pour either a single or double completely hands-free.

While you can get your barista on with this machine, it also comes with pressurized baskets, which will allow less finicky users to get a decent brew out of pre-ground beans.

Unlike the Breville Bambino Plus, there's no automatic steaming with the Bambino. Reviewer Erin was sceptical of its one-hole steam wand — typically you'll be better off with a four-hole as it creates a higher level of pressure — but in testing, the Bambino had no trouble creating velvety-smooth milk.

The machine also comes with a milk jug, which is a nice bonus for an affordable machine, and its wand is more flexible than comparable machines from the likes of De'Longhi.

If you're on a budget, the De'Longhi Stilosa will be a good starting point. Admittedly, you'll need some skill to get great espresso out of this machine. This is because it's manual, meaning there are very few assisted features to make life easier. However, if you're willing to put in the work, the good news is that this machine is more than capable of extracting quality espresso, especially if you pair it with a quality grinder.

Considering the very reasonable price point, it's not surprising that this machine is mostly made of cheap-feeling plastic. But the good news is that under the hood, there's a decent brewer that performs as well as much more expensive machines.

Most impressive was its quality milk wand, which was capable of achieving a fine micro-foam that made delicious lattes and flat whites.

This machine doesn't have a grinder. It's not too hard to make a decent manual espresso machine on a budget, but including a quality grinder (which is absolutely a non-negotiable if you care about great coffee) is expensive. Market-leading grinders can easily cost $300+, so if your machine offers both grinding and brewing capabilities for less than that, it's likely that the grinder is poor quality.

So if you're on a budget and don't mind getting hands-on, the De'Longhi Stilosa is a good work around. Especially if you combine it with a quality hand-grinder like the sub-$100 1Zpresso Q Air.

Tested by our reviews writer (and former barista) Erin, the De'Longhi Stilosa competed with some of the much more premium machines she's reviewed.

With a bit of experimentation and dedication, she found that there’s no reason why you can’t pull consistently delicious shots on the Stilosa. It does require a little know-how, but that's a classic trade-off for the price.

Because the machine doesn't brew to single or double shots, you need to monitor and switch it off yourself. For this, you'll be better off buying a coffee scale so you can tailor your ratios.

You might expect the steam wand on a cheap machine to be flimsy, but if anything, Erin found that the Stilosa’s steam wand can be a touch overzealous.

A former barista, Erin knows her way around a steam wand, and she found that this one needed full concentration during steaming to prevent the milk from becoming over-textured.

However, she did make some awesome lattes in the Stilosa. And for the price, it's one of the top steam wands she's tested.

The Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus is designed around automation, handling weighing, dosing, and grind adjustment for you, so if you're new to home espresso, it removes much of the guesswork. We found its auto-grind-size calibration especially helpful, letting us lock in consistent results with barely any trial and error. This built-in guidance helps streamline the process for beginners, and it's often the number one reason friends and family tell me their machine doesn't work properly. It does, dad, you've just got the wrong grind size. With the Mini Plus, auto-grind-size calibration makes dialing in much easier for new users, so you can reliably pull good shots without trial-and-error adjustments.

With both automatic and manual milk options, the Mini Plus lets you choose how hands-on you want to be. This is especially helpful for beginners learning to texture milk at their own pace.

Compared to the more advanced De'Longhi La Specialista Touch, which provides guided tamping and more complex brewing modes, the Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus stands out for its simplicity and compact footprint. While it lacks in-built tamping and step-by-step drink guidance, it offers a straightforward way to start making espresso at home without requiring a lot of counter space or a steep learning curve.

Something that really sets Ninja coffee makers apart is that their grinder works on an unusual weight-based system. That's the best way, in theory, to ensure you're getting your espresso ratio right every time, and it's why some coffee fanatics will pre-weigh their beans before feeding them into a coffee machine.

The Mini Plus does lack in-built tamping, which is something you'll find in more premium models from Ninja, but it does have a dosing funnel which allows you to catch every drop from the grinder and minimize countertop mess.

Reviewer Erin enjoyed the coffee she made with this machine, but it didn't blow her socks off. She described it as akin to chain coffee shop coffee, which is no bad thing, because the average coffee machine buyer simply wants to replicate their favorite to-go drink at home. But if you know your arabica from your robusta, it might not hit the mark.

There are some pros and cons to the milk steaming with the Ninja Luxe Café line. The milk jug has an in-built spinner to create a vortex in the jug when you're using the automated steaming mode, but you can use the wand manually if you want to learn how to steam by hand.

A big bonus for those who drink a range of milk types is that if you opt for pre-set milk steaming, you can switch between plant and dairy milk settings to prevent oat or soy milk from burning.

This is a halfway house between traditional milk steaming and using a handheld frother to create artificial bubbles in your coffee. Personally, I prefer the automated steam wands you'll find on Breville machines like the Bambino Plus.

But the in-built spinner does have one big bonus in allowing you to create cold foam to pair with your cold coffee. This is something I've not seen in any of the other espresso machines on the market.

If you want a hands-off espresso machine that delivers consistently excellent shots, the Terra Kaffe Demi is a confident pick. The main advantage of superautomatic machines is that they make your coffee from scratch with the touch of a button, but when testing these machines, we frequently find that the finished cup just tastes... bad. That's not an issue reviewer Dan had with the Demi, which allowed him to dial in his perferred settings for espresso and long black coffee, and delivered a consistently delicious brew, cup after cup.

Under the hood, the Demi automates the entire espresso process, from grinding with its conical burr grinder to dosing, tamping, and brewing. In testing, the shots came out reliably rich every single time. Plus, it looks fantastic, and packs in a lot of smarts without being too in-your-face about it.

The main downside is that there's no in-built milk frother. But we tend not to rate the milk frothers which come with superautomatic machines, anyway. You can buy Terra Kaffe's standalone milk frother separately, and use it to make everything from cappuccino to cold foam. The other main issue Dan encountered was that the water tank was on the small side at 47 fluid ounces.

The Demi comes with conical burr grinders, which are typically a better pick than flat burr grinders due to their quieter operation and more consistent results. Because it's hidden away, we tend to find that manufacturers can cut corners when making the grinders for automatic espresso machines, so it's immediately a positive sign that the Demi features conical burrs.

What's less promising is the limited range of grind settings: from one through to five, which is significantly less than the 30+ settings you'll find from alternatives like the Breville Oracle Dual Builer.

The Demi can make five drinks: Espresso, Lungo, Americano, Drip, and Hot Water. So, make that four coffee drinks. It's not the most versatile pick, but in testing we found that our espresso was lively and, most importantly, consistently good.

Dan, a noted coffee snob, said "I was genuinely surprised at how consistent the shots are. Once I had my temperature, strength, and volume dialed in, the shots were as close to perfect as you could expect every time I hit the button."

There's no milk frother here. Instead, you'll have to buy the newly-released Aero Milk Frother if you want a companion to turn your espresso into a cappuccino.

The latest premium contender from Fellow, the Espresso Series 1, is engineered for buyers who want café-level control at home—offering deep shot profile customization and a steam wand that could make a barista blush. If you’re the kind of person who tweaks pre-infusion, flow rate, or pressure profiles for each roast, you’ll be right at home here; the steam wand with its versatile ball joint is a standout for microfoam and serious cappuccino work.

In our testing, dialing in shots with the Series 1 felt more like sculpting than brewing. The results spoke for themselves: the espresso came through with a distinct sweetness and bright acidity that made it hard not to drink the entire shot at once. This isn’t just theoretical control—it’s the real, tangible difference you can taste in the cup, shot after shot.

But there’s a trade-off. Compared to something like the De’Longhi La Specialista Touch, which is more compact and user-friendly, the Series 1 leans into complexity and countertop presence. It’s best for buyers who want to experiment, customize every variable, and don’t mind a learning curve (or a bigger footprint). If that’s you, there’s no better playground—but if you want guided simplicity or a tidier setup, look elsewhere.

There's no built-in grinder with the Fellow Espresso - you'll have to provide your own. Enthusiasts willing to spend the $1.5k to buy this machine likely have a grinder they're happy with already, but if you're building your set-up from scratch, be aware that your budget will have to allow for a grinder as well as brewing device, unless you buy an all-in-one coffee maker.

You can let the Fellow do the heavy lifting when brewing, giving you automatic profiles and step-by-step instructions for brewing that you select with the built-in LCD screen. Or you can dive into the exhaustive settings menu and sort things yourself. Whichever way you want to do it, you'll end up with some awesome brews.

One small complaint we have is the machine's tendency to leave you with wet pucks of coffee grounds once you're finished making your drink. It's not a massive problem, but in theory the Fellow has the technology to produce dry, easily disposable pucks like most other espresso machines of this price.

The steam wand on the Fellow Espresso is one of the best in the business. In fact it produced the single best result we've ever seen for non-dairy milk. It's the kind of milk results that no other machine we know of can match.

Just watch out for the auto-purge function though. It can get in the way of cleaning if you know what you're doing.

Most of this guide is geared towards the average home brewer, but if you want to take it to the next level, the Gaggia Classic E24 is our recommendation. It was tested by our Reviews Editor Peter, a former chef and serious coffee-lover who doesn't mind taking the time to craft coffee the old-fashioned way. His main gripe was that it came with poor-quality tools, but these are easily replaced.

This machine lacks a lot of the assists you'll find with Breville and De'Longhi machines. There's no PID, no thermoblock, and you'll have to start and stop the extraction yourself.

The plus side of this is that you get complete control over your shot of coffee. Some machines try and steer you because they assume they know better, but if you've got the know-how, this machine will leave you to it and not intervene.

There's no grinder to be seen here. You'll want to pair this compact espresso machine with a quality home grinder such as the Eureka Mignon Specialita, which just so happens to be the grinder we used during testing.

As I said, this machine leaves all the hard work to you. It's a single-boiler without a PID. What does this mean? Well, it heats up the entire tank instead of the amount of water needed for a specific dose, and it won't monitor and adjust the temperature of your coffee during extraction. You can add a PID if you choose to modify this machine, but if you go as is, you're temperature-surfing to hit the optimum extraction.

Due to its larger brass boiler and brass group head, the Gaggia now offers higher levels of temperature stability (a common problem in machines without PID). Peter found that it was more than capable of extracting complex, punchy espresso. "I tested the Gaggia with a range of beans, including light-medium, medium and dark roasts, using washed, wet-hulled, honey-processed and natural processing. The E24 did justice to the lot."

Peter made some brilliant lattes in this machine. Its steam wand is more powerful than any other in this guide (aside perhaps from the Meraki), because (like a commercial machine) it works with a boiler to hit high pressure on demand.

This means you'll be able to create glossy microfoam for a flat white or cappuccino in a matter of seconds. Peter found that it could make a flat white in ten seconds flat. However, as you're working with one boiler, you'll need to 'purge' your machine to get rid of the overheated water after milk steaming is finished. The temperature will be too high to go back to brewing espresso.

I'm pretty cagey with who I let review espresso machines for Tom's Guide. When I bought my first espresso machine, I couldn't tell if my failure to get a good espresso out of my fancy new gadget was the machine's fault, or human error. If I'd written a review of that machine, it wouldn't have been very fair on the reader, or the machine!

But now I've got five years of testing, well over 30 coffee machine reviews, and a Specialty Coffee Association qualification under my belt. My friends are always asking me questions about coffee, why their machine isn't working for them, or which they should buy, so I'd like to think I can be that person to our readers, too.

Fortunately, at Tom's Guide, I'm not alone. We've got a brilliant team of experienced testers with almost 20 years of coffee expertise between us.

As a former barista (and current product tester), I've spent a lot of time getting hands-on with espresso machines.

After a combined three years at two of the biggest coffee chains and a year at an artisan independent coffee shop, I can detect a well-balanced shot when I taste it, and can also interpret the culprit behind a poor extraction, be it low pressure, grind size, or poor temperature controls.

Spending three years making hundreds of coffees a day might make a person gag at the sight of lattes, but coffee still holds a special place in my heart.

My favorite drink is an oat milk flat white, made with Kenyan or Ethiopian beans.

I’m Tom’s Guide's Reviews Editor and I’ve been an espresso enthusiast for almost a decade now.

As a former chef, I started using commercial espresso machines to make tiramisu while working in an Italian restaurant, and that’s where my fascination with 9-bar pressure began. And it hasn’t stopped since.

Fun fact: every job I’ve held since has given me access to espresso machines — oddly enough, that includes when I worked at an energy company, where we had a commercial Expobar machine plumbed into the office kitchen!

These days, I spend large chunks of my day testing out the latest and greatest coffee gear, from coffee grinders and weighing scales through to pour-over drippers and, of course, espresso machines.

I’ve used home espresso machines from Breville/Sage, Rancilio, Gaggia, De’Longhi, Diletta and more. Through my years of testing (and tasting), I have the experience to know when a machine performs as it should and whether or not it’s worth your hard-earned cash.

We test a ton of coffee gear at Tom's Guide, and not everything can make it to the final guide. If I don't include something, that doesn't necessarily mean we don't recommend it, so if none of the machines listed above take your fancy, you might get along better with one of these tried-and-tested options.

We don't tend to rate superautomatic espresso machines, but the KF8 surprised us. In fact, it used to feature in this guide until we tested the Terra Kaffe Demi.

Read the full KitchenAid KF8 Coffee Machine review

If you're on a budget, Casabrews machines are worth a look. The trade-off is in the built quality, but in our tests, we did find that they're capable of making a tasty espresso.

Read the full Casabrews Ultra Coffee Machine review

Newcomer to the espresso game Meraki is offering a stunning range of features for the price. The downside? It's still in development, with some tweaks having now been made to the model we first tested, which means we can't recommend it until we've tested the new and improved model.

Read the full Meraki Espresso Machine review

The De’Longhi Dedica Duo is neat and compact, but it's quite expensive for what it is, especially when the Stilosa is cheaper and just as capable. However, you can't deny that it's a looker, which could make it a contender if you're setting up a coffee nook.

Read the full De’Longhi Dedica Duo review

Our love of the Breville Bambino Plus is very well documented, but when we added its cheaper counterpart, the Bambino, to this guide, we felt that we didn't need both here. The Plus is incredible, with automated steaming and powerful extraction, but it's slightly less good value for money.

Read the full Breville Bambino Plus review

De’Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo (★★★★☆)

Looking for a budget-friendly espresso machine with character and an in-built grinder? The De’Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo is practically in a league of its own, offering specs that punch well above its weight. The only reason it's not in this guide is that we love the Specialista Touch more.

Read the full De’Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo review

KitchenAid Semi Automatic Espresso Machine (★★★★☆)

The KitchenAid Semi Automatic Espresso Machine with Burr Grinder is the entry-level option in KitchenAid's line of coffee makers. It's a mid-price, high-quality option, but it lacks a lot of the automated features you'll see from options like Breville and De'Longhi.

Read the full KitchenAid Semi Automatic Espresso Machine review

With some trial and error though, Reviews Editor Peter hit his stride with the Silvia. After some experimentation he said he was "actually a little taken aback at how nice espresso shots tasted." If you've got a refined palate and espresso known-how, this could be a good option.

Read the full Rancilio Silvia (V6) Espresso Machine review

De’Longhi Dedica Duo Espresso Machine (★★★☆☆)

The De'Longhi Dedica Duo is a good espresso machine capable of making pleasant cold brew for just $299. Even so, it's the same price as the fantastic Breville Bambino and $150 pricier than our favorite budget machine, the De’Longhi Stilosa.

Read the full De’Longhi Dedica Duo Espresso Machine review

Philips Barista Brew Espresso Machine (★★★☆☆)

The Philips Barista Brew is Philips' first attempt at an automatic coffee machine. The rest of the line is superautomatic, and start at quite affordable prices. When we tested the Barista Brew, we didn't have an issue with the quality of its extraction or construction, it just struggles to break through the very crowded market of machines that look, cost, and perform almost exactly the same.

Read the full Philips Barista Brew Espresso Machine review

You probably didn't come to this guide looking for a wireless coffee maker, but this non-electric option is very affordable, super portable, and ideal for travel. It uses a valve to create the pressure needed to extract espresso, and we were really impressed by how well it worked.

The Terra Kaffe is super smart. It claims to feature AI tech that will personalize your brew to your specific preferences, and it certainly looks space-age. The price will rule it out of contention for most people though, and it's also a very large option.

The Philips 3200 Series LatteGo is one of the most affordable superautomatic espresso machines on the market. It feels plasticky in use and the milk dispenser will struggle to compete with more expensive options, but if you want a one-and-done option that doesn't cost the earth, it's a good choice.

Read the full Philips 3200 Series LatteGo review

You can make any kind of coffee drink you like with this automatic machine from Ninja, but the mixed quality of the outputs prevented us from awarding a higher rating.

Read our full Ninja AutoBarista Pro review

One to avoid this time around — it makes coffee, but there's not much to say about it. It costs far too much money for the quality of espresso that it spits out, even if the device itself does look pretty special.

Read the full Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series review

We review a lot of espresso machines at Tom's Guide. Very few of them make it into our buying guides, but you can see a comprehensive list of other models we've tested at the bottom of this guide.

When it comes to testing espresso machines, there's a lot of room for human error. In order to minimize this, I work closely with a team of true coffee experts, from former baristas to serious home baristas. Every review you'll read on Tom's Guide will be from a true espresso enthusiast who can tell their flat whites from their cappuccinos and their arabica from their robusta.

We consider a huge range of factors when evaluating espresso machines. Here's a non-exhaustive list of the things we test for:

Ease of use: You shouldn't have to be a pro to work an espresso machine. These appliances are designed to make life easier, so while it's fair to expect a learning curve if you opt for a manual machine with lots of hands-on features, we mark machines down for any quirks or fiddly features that will make day-to-day use harder for the average buyer.

Ease of cleaning: Some machines are splashy, messy, and get greasy from the touch of a button. These are workhorses, sure, but they're also meant to look nice, so we evaluate whether they spill grounds, splatter milk, or will require any major upkeep with each review.

Value for money: Even a budget espresso machine can be expensive, so we always consider whether a machine is priced competitively when putting it to the test. If we wouldn't recommend our friends spend their money on a machine, we wouldn't recommend it to you, either.

Grinding: If a machine has an in-built grinder, we put it through the same testing that we use when evaluating the best coffee grinders. After all, the quality of your grinder plays a massive part in achieving a good extraction. It's the single most important part of any espresso-brewing process. We evaluate the range of grind sizes on offer with every machine (you'll want a very fine consistency, but this will vary depending on the bean you use), as well as how much coffee a machine grinds automatically. A lot of enthusiasts brew using ratios, so we like to weigh the grounds before we brew for good measure.

Brewing: Albeit an important step, this is also the simplest to test. Whether a machine can brew well is dependent on the performance of the grinder, but we know we've got a quality coffee if it brews at that sweet spot between 190 to 200°F (88 and 93°C) and we get between 25-30ml of espresso. We use a coffee scale to test this, just to be extra thorough.

Taste test: Metrics aside, it's all in the taste-test. We buy high-quality coffee (currently, we're using a subscription to Hard Lines' specialty coffee) that's freshly-roasted to give our machines the best possible chance of brewing a brilliant espresso. And if it tastes too bitter or too tart, we know it's not the beans' fault! If the coffee tastes too grassy, it suggests the machine doesn't brew hot enough, and if it's burnt-tasting, that's a sign that it's not got good temperature regulation and is scorching our grounds.

Milk steaming: Steam wands need to be powerful, ergonomic and responsive. A great wand will not only heat your milk but also help to create a powerful vortex, which will add texture and incorporate air into your milk jug. I'll get more into how to use a steam wand below, but you best believe that if former barista Erin can't get a good texture from a steam wand, there's no hope for a home user.

Super-automatic espresso machines will often feature milk dispensers that automatically froth your milk and pour it into your mug. This is really convenient if you don't like the idea of learning to steam milk by hand, but just so we're clear, these machines don't steam your milk. They simply heat it and inject some bubbles as they pour into your cup. It gets the job done, but it's not going to compete with a coffee shop-quality flat white.

Longevity: You need to be prepared to look after an espresso machine. They block easily if you don't descale regularly, and your group head and steam wand will need to be flushed out periodically. This aside, we've also tried machines that simply don't feel like they're built to last. Where possible, we like to hang onto a top pick for prolonged home use and testing. That way, we can update our guide if it doesn't seem built to last. Our number one, the De'Longhi La Specialista Opera, is currently living with Erin as her home machine, allowing us to continue to evaluate its position in this guide.

This question used to be a lot more simple to answer: there's manual, and there's super-automatic! However, things have changed a lot in the last few years, and now there's an increasing number of machines that sit somewhere in between.

In truth, it would be easier to characterize types of espresso machine as a spectrum, all the way from lever pump machines like La Pavoni to one-touch super-automatics like Jura.

But to make life easier, I've divided the domestic machines in this guide into three categories:

Espresso machines are pretty complicated, which is why I did a dedicated Specialty Coffee Association course before compiling this guide. While I’ve tried to make it as accessible as possible, there is some terminology you might need to learn to understand the reviews below. Here are the ABC's of espresso machines.

If you’re completely new to espresso machines, the thing you have to ask yourself is: “how much time do I want to spend, how much skill do I have, and how much am I prepared to put into this?"

I posed this question to Lucy Dunstan, Product Manager at SMEG and La Pavoni. “It’s quite simple really, it’s all about extracting the flavor from your coffee,” she told me.

“There’s a scientific process for making an espresso. It has to be between 88 and 93°C [190 to 200°F], you have to put about 9 bars of pressure on it, and you want to extract between 25 and 30ml of liquid. So what all these machines do is offer a way of controlling that process.”

There are so many variables that stand between your machine and a perfect espresso. This includes the beans you use, how you grind them, the volume of grounds in your portafilter, the pressure you use when tamping, the temperature stability of your machine, the water pressure exerted, the volume of water pushed into your puck… that’s a non-exhaustive list, and it’s before we even get into milk steaming!

There are so many variables that stand between your machine and a perfect espresso

Here’s what I wish I’d known when I bought my first espresso machine: The more automated features you opt for, the fewer variables you’ll need to worry about. “Sometimes with espresso machines, an entry-level price will actually require more skill,” says Dunstan.

“If you’re completely new to espresso machines, the thing you have to ask yourself is: how much time do I want to spend, how much skill do I have, and how much am I prepared to put into this? So you’re either someone who doesn’t have a lot of time to spend on making your coffee, or you want to delve into that world where you’re getting hands-on."

There's an unfortunate irony with espresso machines. You can get good espresso with a cheaper machine, but to do so, you'll need to learn the ins and outs of how these machines work. For the entry-level buyer without much knowledge, you'll often have to spend a lot more on a super-capable machine that will take all the hard work out of the equation.

It doesn't make much sense, right? Coffee enthusiasts can get away with spending $200 on a basic espresso machine because they've got the skill to use it properly, but if you're just dipping your toes in the water? Well, prepare to spend at least $500. It's no wonder why so many people opt for a pod machine like a Keurig or a Nespresso!

Fortunately, the market is catching up. An increasing amount of espresso machines feature assisted settings that will remove some of the variables that can mess up your espresso. This includes automated grinding that controls the volume of coffee dispensed into your portafilter, automated tamping for an even pressure, and even hands-free steam wands that will texture your milk for you.

The majority of the machines I've included in this machine fit into this automatic category in some sense. I think they're the best option for most people, allowing you to learn as you use the machine and get hands-on if you wish, but also taking the reins when you just want a low-effort espresso.

You'll see in the products included I've mentioned how many bars of pressure they each have, but what does this mean, and does it even matter? Well, the short answer is no. You won't necessarily see a better extraction from a machine with 20 bars over a machine with 15. This is because the ideal pressure needed for espresso is 9 bars.

I asked Luke Lane, Training & Events Manager for Sage Appliances, to explain the significance of pressure for espresso machines. "You want to hit 9 bars for optimal extraction," he told me.

"If the pressure is too low, you'll bring out grassy flavors. The pressure won't bring out the sugars from your beans.

"Too high, and your coffee will have a bitter, burnt taste."

If all you need to make a great espresso is 9 bars of pressure, so I asked Lane why so many espresso machines have more?

"Think of it like a car," Lane told me. "You don't want to drive it at top speed all the time, but driving in a comfortable range of what your car is capable of will mean it's not constantly being run flat-out."

He explained that despite the maximum pressure of any machine, they'll use OPVs (which stands for over pressure valves) to keep espresso extraction running at a consistent 9 bars of pressure.

So, while higher pressure doesn't necessarily mean a machine is any better, you might not want to buy a machine with a maximum output of 9 bars, or it could lead to a shorter lifespan for your machine.

Most espresso machines will come with four baskets: two single and two double, with a mix of double-walled and single-walled constructions. I'll explain the difference between single-walled and double-walled below, but what's the significance of your basket size and capacity?

Luke Lane, Training & Events Manager for Sage Appliances, explained it to me: "There are two main basket widths: 54mm, which features on Sage / Breville's Barista range, and 58mm, which features on our Jet range."

"58mm is considered to be commercial-grade. The larger and shallower basket will give you marginally better results because you're more easily able to permeate all of the grounds inside your basket."

After testing countless espresso machines, I don't think my palette is quite so attuned that I could turn my nose up at an espresso from a 54mm basket. But it's useful to know if you want to replace or upgrade any parts of your machine what size portafilter baskets the group head will fit.

Single-walled and double-walled baskets, also known respectively as unpressurized and pressurized, are included with your espresso machine to give you options. As a general rule of thumb, you'll get better results from a pressurized basket if you're using pre-ground coffee. It will help you overcome some of the shortcomings of a grind size that's too coarse, or coffee that's less fresh. But if you want to taste the authentic flavor of your fresh-ground beans, a single-walled basket is the way to go.

In our reviews, we always use fresh-ground coffee, so we stick to single-walled baskets for the majority of our testing.

When I asked him to explain how pressurized baskets work, Luke Lane, Training & Events Manager for Sage Appliances, said "Think of a group of people running down a hall and having to go through a door." He explained, "That's what the double-walled basket does. It creates pressure by restricting the flow of your coffee, forcing it to build up more flavor and crema than you'd have been able to achieve with a less fresh coffee."

We've done a thorough explainer on this in our guide to pressurized coffee baskets — how do they work and when should you use them? The short answer? They can act as a cheat code to a better espresso if you're not working with the ideal gear, but a machine with an in-built grinder shouldn't need one.

The vast majority of domestic espresso machines use thermoblock technology to heat water on demand. But how does it work, and what are the pros and cons?

There are very few single boiler machines on the market, but the Rancilio Silvia is one of them. Boiler machines will heat your water and keep it at temperature for as and when you decide to use it. A single-boiler uses one boiler for both the group head and the steam wand, which require different temperatures and therefore will need to you purge excess hot water as you use different elements of the machine.

Dual boilers have one boiler for the group head, and another for your steam wand. They're not super popular for domestic, and I've not included a dual-boiler in this guide. They have a higher energy consumption because they keep your water hot for more precision and stability.

What about thermoblock? I asked Lucy Dunstan, Product Manager at SMEG and La Pavoni, to explain. “A thermoblock is a heated metal block with one or more pipes running through it that will rapidly heat water on demand," she explained.

"They’re usually very compact so they don’t take up much space, meaning they can be fitted in smaller machines, and they’re more energy efficient [than a dual boiler].”

“So the advantage is that they’re fast, small, and energy-efficient. The disadvantage is that they offer less temperature consistency than a dual boiler machine.

"And they can, over time, be susceptible to limescale, so they may not last as long. Whereas if you buy a dual boiler La Pavoni machine, and you look after it, I’d expect it to last you a lifetime.”

Millie was the Managing Editor of Buying Guides at Tom's Guide. Previously Managing Editor of Homes, she's been reviewing home tech for over five years, testing everything from coffee makers to the latest vacuum cleaners.

With particular expertise in cookware and kitchen appliances, you'll struggle to find an air fryer Millie hasn't tested. She's traveled the world reporting on the latest home innovations and product launches, learning how to use pizza ovens from Pizzaiolos in Naples, and touring the De'Longhi factory in Venice. Millie is also an SCA-Certified barista.

When she's not reporting on home and appliance trends, Millie loves watching live music. She's currently learning the guitar - naturally, she plays a Fender.

#3067. DeepMind’s AI agents found cheaper quantum algorithms, and proved them

Teams of Gemini 4 agents cut a fusion simulation's cost nearly 12-fold, with every result mathematically proved.

Google DeepMind’s illustration for its research on AI-discovered quantum algorithms.

Google DeepMind and Google Quantum AI used teams of Gemini 4 agents to find more efficient quantum algorithms for fusion, chemistry and drug-design problems. Each result was proved correct in the Lean theorem prover, because the circuits are too large to test on today’s computers.

Google DeepMind says teams of AI agents have found faster quantum algorithms for problems in fusion energy, chemistry and drug design. The agents, running on Gemini 4, proved each result correct with Lean, a tool that checks mathematical proofs, the lab said on Monday.

The proofs matter because the circuits are too big to test. They need thousands of qubits, far beyond what classical computers can simulate or today’s quantum chips can run.

The biggest gain came in a fusion problem. The agents cut the cost of a quantum calculation for laser-driven fusion fuel by 11.8 times, and its memory from 5,650 to 4,338 error-corrected qubits, DeepMind says.

They also made a simulation of a light-sensitive molecule about eight times cheaper. For Cytochrome P450, an enzyme that breaks down most medicines, the cost fell 2.5 times. A widely used maths routine became more than 290 times cheaper.

Separate agent teams worked on each problem and shared verified ideas in a common notebook. Every four hours, they met in a virtual conference to debate and compare approaches. The work, with Google Quantum AI, used Google’s most powerful model, Gemini 4 Carbon.

An outside checker re-ran every proof so agents could not game the tests, according to the paper. That risk is real: in a DeepMind experiment in September, 14% of agents cheated on Lean maths problems.

DeepMind cautions that the simulations would still need far more resources than the first error-corrected quantum computers will offer. It has open-sourced its Lean library and results, building on its 2024 work to trim quantum circuits with AlphaTensor-Quantum. Earlier this month, its agents also proved Signal’s encryption code correct, and Google Quantum AI tested a key quantum effect on up to 105 qubits.

#3066. RayNeo Black Friday deals: AR smart glasses that turn your Mac and iPhone into a 307-inch screen

Still waiting for tech like the Vision Pro, but in normal everyday glasses and sunglasses? The industry leader in AR glasses shipments has something to say.

The best Apple accessories share a distinct DNA: immaculate industrial design, lightweight ergonomics, tactile physical precision, and friction-free performance that feels native from minute one. Launched globally this fall, the RayNeo GT Max and RayNeo iO pair premium materials and bleeding-edge optics with the one thing Mac and iPhone owners actually want from a display accessory — plug it in, and it works.

RayNeo isn’t a small player making a big claim here. The company took the No. 1 spot in global AR smart glasses shipments across the first half of 2026, with 24.8% market share according to IDC and 23.9% according to Counterpoint Research.

Its Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale is live now through November 30, with the flagship GT Max at $335 (down from $429), the lighter GT at $249 (down from $329), and the camera-free iO smart glasses at $389 (down from $499). Everything is available on RayNeo.com and Amazon US.

Watching a movie on your iPhone is convenient, but craning your neck for a comfortable view is hardly cinematic. Having a premium AR display in sunglasses form, without packing a bulky mixed-reality headset or computing puck, opens up entirely new possibilities.

The RayNeo GT Max and RayNeo GT connect to your device over a single USB-C cable. Instead of clunky goggles, the GT Series puts a massive virtual display — 59 degrees of field of view on GT Max, to be exact — into a sleek, understated sunglasses design that blends into coffee shops and airport lounges at just 68 to 78 grams. That single USB-C connection carries uncompressed video and powers the glasses directly: no secondary battery packs to carry, no charging anxiety, and zero wireless lag.

One thing to check before you buy: the glasses need a device that outputs video over USB-C (DisplayPort Alt Mode). That covers the iPhone 15, 16 and 17 series, Macs from 2015 onward with USB-C, iPad from the 10th generation on, and USB-C handhelds like the Steam Deck. The iPhone 16e, 17e and iPhone Air have USB-C ports but don’t output video over them, so they aren’t supported. Consoles and older Lightning devices need RayNeo’s HDMI adapter.

Both GT Max and GT use dual 1080p Micro-OLED panels, delivering a Full HD image to each eye with ultra-smooth 120Hz refresh rates in 2D mode. GT Max adds 38 pixels per degree, 98% DCI-P3 cinematic color coverage, and TÜV Rheinland triple eye-comfort certification. Each model offers three selectable virtual screen sizes, depending on how immersed you want to be:

GT Max’s wider field of view provides a more expansive picture, while GT offers a featherweight design. For travel, the appeal is simple: an immaculate 307-inch personal theater that slips right into your daily bag alongside your Apple gear.

The GT Series also functions as an instant, private external display for a USB-C Mac. That makes the glasses invaluable far beyond streaming media, especially when you need an expansive, shoulder-surfer-proof dual-monitor workspace on a flight, train, or co-working desk.

Both GT and GT Max include three native 3DoF hardware display modes, meaning you can position your virtual screen around your head:

Because the tracking runs on dedicated silicon inside the glasses, none of it taxes the Mac or iPhone you’re plugged into. The glasses draw minimal power directly from the connected device and include a four-speaker spatial acoustic array co-tuned by Bang & Olufsen, with a directional Whisper Mode that cuts sound leakage on a plane or in an office.

GT Max also comes in three sizes based on inter-pupillary distance (IPD) — small for under 64mm, medium for 64–67mm, large for over 67mm — ensuring a tailored, comfortable fit.

If an everyday display frame came out of Cupertino today, it would look like RayNeo iO. Rather than heavy visors, iO pairs with your iPhone through the RayNeo app to project glanceable, contextual intelligence into genuine everyday eyewear.

iO uses a high-efficiency binocular MicroLED optical engine to float high-contrast green text into your sightline, presenting a virtual image equivalent to a 33-inch screen viewed from two meters away. With peak eye-level brightness rated at 1,300 nits, reading notes and prompts stays crystal clear even under direct midday sun without occluding your real-world surroundings. The waveguide is 97% transparent and the optical engine is hidden inside the frame, so from the outside these read as ordinary glasses — most people never clock them as smart eyewear at all.

For presentations and pitches, the built-in teleprompter scrolls your notes in sync with your natural speaking cadence, so you keep your eyes locked on your audience instead of looking down at your phone. During face-to-face meetings or international travel, the glasses deliver live subtitles and two-way translation right on the lenses, with support for 55 languages and 109 accents at roughly one second of latency.

Beyond live translation and teleprompting, RayNeo iO acts as a constantly evolving heads-up companion. RayNeo pushes frequent over-the-air (OTA) software updates, continually expanding what the glasses can do throughout your day.

Just now coming to iO is heads-up turn-by-turn navigation, which projects glanceable directional arrows, street names, and real-time transit alerts directly into your line of sight. Whether you’re walking through a new city or cycling down busy streets, you can navigate without holding your iPhone in front of you or looking down at your wrist. Alongside navigation, regular software updates continue to introduce new lifestyle tools, customizable notification filters, and contextual dashboard widgets that keep the hardware feeling fresh.

There’s more coming in December, too: RayNeo is opening the iO SDK to the public, so third-party apps — and community-built ones from people with no development background — start landing on the platform shortly after the holidays.

A four-microphone array with a bone-conduction sensor captures clear audio for automated meeting minutes and AI summaries that extract key action items. RayNeo V1 and Google Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite are built in and free out of the box — no subscription required for everyday voice response, contextual reasoning, and ambient assistance. On the temple, an intuitive Smart Crown lets you scroll notifications and highlight key moments with familiar, physical micro-precision.

The titanium frames weigh just 33 grams and are rated IP54 for dust and water resistance, with a battery good for up to two days of typical use, 6.2 hours of continuous live translation, and a 25-minute charge to 80%.

iO supports Bluetooth 5.4 and carries Apple’s MFi (Made for iPhone) certification. It also has no speakers by design — which sounds like an omission until you realize what it buys you. RayNeo’s ultra-slim titanium temple arms sit flush against your ears and leave them completely free, so your AirPods stay in with Spatial Audio, Transparency Mode, and Active Noise Cancellation untouched for music and calls, while iO handles your heads-up visual intelligence.

#3065. Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous

Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”

These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.

In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might lead

• Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress

AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?

AI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.

The intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.

Powerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.

Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.

An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.

Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

There’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”

In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”

These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

Consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives.

The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

This fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “The Superintelligence Delusion.”

Cal Newport is a computer science professor at Georgetown University where he is also a founding faculty member of the Center for Digital Ethics. He's the author of multiple bestselling books about human flourishing in a technological world and is the host of The Cal Newport Show podcast.

The thing that bothers me is that AI people believe that intelligence can be reached by just digesting the entire internet. Instead, human intelligence includes a learning process starting at childhood by careful learning from other kids, and parents and other adults during play, observing the reaction on crying while hungry or anxiety when left alone, and so on. The empty brain of the newborn is filled with at least two decades of human interaction before it can deliver Nobel prize level intelligence. Have fun learning all this from the internet instead.

Concerns about AI are legitimate. These systems can be used to intensify surveillance, generate convincing disinformation, facilitate cyberattacks, and concentrate economic and political power. More capable systems may introduce additional risks, particularly when deployed without adequate testing or oversight.

We should not dismiss these dangers. But neither should we treat catastrophe as inevitable simply because a technology is powerful.

The answer to risk is not blind faith. It is serious evaluation, independent testing, appropriate safeguards, accountability, and governance proportionate to the potential harm. High-risk applications warrant greater scrutiny than routine uses.

I think the current transformer attention method is not the method to reach ASI. There will need to be something else that pushes it forward. From my understanding the large data corpus is really just an advanced prediction system. Something will need to come along to actually understand concepts terms and know how to reason about things.
